Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
SignificanceHigh-energy electron beams are powerful tools for examining materials and biological systems, but it remains unclear how strongly they can interact with individual quantum systems in solids. Unlocking this interaction could enable electron-...
tldr: This paper explores using solid-state spins (NV centers) as quantum sensors for high-energy electron beams, demonstrating spin-dependent fluorescence changes under electron irradiation.
motivation: To understand and harness the interaction between high-energy electron beams and individual quantum systems in solids, enabling new sensing modalities for electron microscopy and beam diagnostics.
method: The authors experimentally expose NV centers in diamond to focused electron beams and measure spin-state-dependent fluorescence, analyzing the effect of electron dose and energy on spin initialization and readout.
result: They observe that electron beams can initialize and read out NV spin states, with contrast and fidelity sufficient for sensing applications, and characterize the interaction cross-section.
conclusion: Solid-state spins can serve as quantum sensors for electron beams, offering high spatial resolution and sensitivity, with potential for integration into electron microscopes.

title: Characterizing Resources For Multiparameter Estimation Of Su(2) And Su(1,1) Unitaries
authors: Shaowei Du, Shuheng Liu, Frank E. S. Steinhoff, And Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2130 (2026).

We analyze the task of estimating a multi-parameter unitary belonging to the [MATH] or [MATH] groups, in a two-bosonic-mode scenario and investigate the scaling of the precision in terms of the total particle number. For the [MATH] case, the total particle number is conserved by the evolution and we discuss optimal states in fixed-[MATH] subspaces, identifying eigenstates of [MATH] as useful resources, even allowing simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. In the [MATH] case instead, the conserved quantity is the particle number difference between the two modes, and we identify useful probe states in the sector with an equal number of particles in the two modes. These states are analogous to the [MATH] case and would also allow simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. We then consider the more pragmatic scenario of an estimation via expectation values of time-evolved observables, which we restrict to be the first two moments of the generators. We analyze the maximal precision achievable in this setting and we find that the twin-Fock state emerges in both the [MATH] and the [MATH] cases as the only one potentially allowing Heisenberg scaling for the estimation of two out of the three parameters. As a complement, we also consider other probe states with fluctuating number of particles, with measurements restricted to quadratic expressions in the mode operators. In this scenario, simultaneous Heisenberg scaling in multiple parameters seems mostly forbidden, with the only exception being an input two-mode squeezed state for the estimation of a two-parameter [MATH]. This extends to the multiparameter scenario the well-established intuition that the performance of a [MATH] interferometer can be enhanced by a prior [MATH] operation.

.
tldr: Analyzes multiparameter estimation of SU(2) and SU(1,1) unitaries in two-bosonic-mode systems, identifying optimal probe states for Heisenberg-limited precision.
motivation: To characterize quantum resources for simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters in unitary evolutions, which is crucial for quantum metrology and sensing.
method: Theoretical analysis of precision scaling with total particle number, considering optimal states in fixed-number subspaces and practical measurement schemes using expectation values of generators.
result: Eigenstates of J_z (SU(2)) and analogous states (SU(1,1)) allow simultaneous Heisenberg scaling for all three parameters; twin-Fock state enables Heisenberg scaling for two parameters under restricted measurements.
conclusion: Identifies specific probe states that achieve optimal multiparameter estimation, extending single-parameter intuitions to the multiparameter regime.

title: Classical Shadows For Sample-efficient Measurements Of Gauge-invariant Observables
authors: Jacob Bringewatt, Henry Froland, Andreas Elben, And Niklas Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2127 (2026).

Classical shadows provide a versatile framework for estimating many properties of quantum states from repeated, randomly chosen measurements without requiring full quantum state tomography. When prior information is available, such as knowledge of symmetries of states and operators, this knowledge can be exploited to significantly improve sample efficiency. In this work, we develop three classical shadow protocols for [MATH] lattice gauge theory, where a dual formulation enables a rigorous analysis of resource requirements, including both circuit depth and sample complexity. Our approaches can offer exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, albeit at the cost of increased circuit complexity. While our analysis is restricted to [MATH] lattice gauge theory, our approach offers a blueprint for similar protocols for more general lattice gauge theory models which are currently at the forefront of quantum simulation efforts.

.
tldr: Develops classical shadow protocols for lattice gauge theory that exploit gauge symmetry to exponentially improve sample efficiency.
motivation: Estimating gauge-invariant observables in lattice gauge theory is crucial for quantum simulation but sample-inefficient without symmetry information.
method: Proposes three classical shadow protocols that incorporate gauge symmetry via a dual formulation, analyzing circuit depth and sample complexity.
result: Achieves exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, at the cost of increased circuit complexity.
conclusion: The approach provides a blueprint for efficient measurement of gauge-invariant observables in more general lattice gauge theories.

title: What Can We Do In A Symmetry-constrained Perspective? The Importance Of The Total Charge’s Status In Quantum Reference Frame Frameworks
authors: Guilhem Doat And Augustin Vanrietvelde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2126 (2026).

The study of quantum reference frames has received renewed interest over the last years, leading to the parallel development of non-equivalent frameworks by different communities. We clarify the differences between these frameworks. At the mathematical level, they mainly differ in the kind of symmetry (either weak or strong) employed to constrain the system. We show that this mathematical difference corresponds to a fundamental physical question: whether the global charge associated to the symmetry group is accessible to symmetry-constrained observers. In this context, we formulate a definition of a perspective in terms of operational capacities, or lack thereof. Turning to consequences of adopting either approach, we discuss how adopting the weak approach induces an ambiguity in the momenta included in each perspective and bars from defining reversible QRF transformations. We then review and analyze the existing arguments motivating each approach, and show how they bear upon the problem of charge accessibility. Finally, we introduce a simple operational scenario in which upholding two reasonable physical postulates leads to the conclusion that internal observers could measure the global charge by 1/ performing a relativized interference measurement and 2/ classically communicating.

.
tldr: The paper clarifies differences between quantum reference frame frameworks based on weak vs. strong symmetry constraints, linking them to the accessibility of global charge.
motivation: Different communities have developed non-equivalent frameworks for quantum reference frames, and the paper aims to clarify their mathematical and physical distinctions.
method: The authors analyze the mathematical differences (weak vs. strong symmetry) and connect them to whether the global charge is accessible to symmetry-constrained observers. They introduce a definition of perspective based on operational capacities and review existing arguments.
result: Adopting the weak approach induces ambiguity in momenta and prevents reversible QRF transformations. The authors show that internal observers could measure the global charge via a relativized interference measurement and classical communication.
conclusion: The choice of symmetry constraint has physical implications for charge accessibility and the structure of quantum reference frames, with the weak approach limiting reversible transformations.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies the dynamical Lie algebras of QAOA circuits, providing bounds on DLA dimensions and proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the trainability and expressiveness of variational quantum algorithms is crucial for their practical use; barren plateaus hinder training, and DLA analysis offers a theoretical tool to characterize them.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on DLA dimensions and centers for general graphs, then explicitly compute the DLA structure for cycle and complete graphs using representation theory.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a center and a semisimple part isomorphic to copies of sl(2), and the cost function variance is computed, proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is determined and an explicit basis given.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA DLAs, advancing the theoretical understanding of barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum Hypergraph States: A Review
authors: Dagmar Bruß And Chiara Macchiavello Davide Poderini
abstract: Quantum hypergraph states extend the well-studied class of graph states by taking into account multi-qubit interactions through hyperedges. They provide a powerful framework to represent a family of quantum states with genuine multipartite entanglement. In this review, we provide a compact overview of the formal structure, entanglement characteristics, and operational relevance of hypergraph states in quantum information theory. We begin by introducing their mathematical foundations and generalizations of the stabilizer formalism. A central focus is placed on their entanglement properties, including the classification under local unitary and stochastic local operations with classical communication, the quantification of multipartite entanglement, and detection techniques via entanglement witnesses. We also explore other nonclassical features of hypergraph states, such as contextuality and genuine multipartite nonlocality, derived from stabilizer-based Bell-type inequalities. Additional attention is given to the role of hypergraph states in error correction, and as a computational resource in measurement-based quantum computation, and to their non-stabilizer character, quantified via resource-theoretic measures of quantum magic. Finally we review their generalization to higher dimensions, i.e. to qudits and continuous variables.
tldr: A review of quantum hypergraph states, covering their mathematical structure, entanglement properties, nonclassical features, and applications in error correction and measurement-based quantum computation.
motivation: Hypergraph states generalize graph states to multi-qubit interactions, offering a richer framework for studying multipartite entanglement and quantum information protocols.
method: The paper provides a compact overview of the formal structure, stabilizer formalism, entanglement classification under LU and SLOCC, and detection via witnesses, as well as contextuality and nonlocality from Bell inequalities.
result: It summarizes known results on entanglement quantification, magic resource theory, and generalizations to qudits and continuous variables.
conclusion: Hypergraph states are a versatile family with genuine multipartite entanglement and operational relevance, though the review does not present new results.

title: Hamiltonian And Double-bracket Flow Formulations Of Quantum Measurements
authors: Aarón Villanueva And Luis Pedro García-Pintos
abstract: We introduce a framework that unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket (DB) gradient flows. We do so by providing explicit expressions for stochastic Hamiltonians that produce state dynamics identical to those that happen during continuous quantum measurements. When such dynamical processes are integrated over sufficiently long time intervals, they yield the same results and statistics as during wavefunction collapse. That is, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained (stochastic) Hamiltonian dynamics. Alternatively, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as DB gradient flows determined by derivatives of (stochastic) potentials defined in terms of observables with direct physical interpretations. The gradient flows minimize the variance of the monitored observable. Our derivations hold for general monitoring described by non-Hermitian jump processes. We show that such reinterpretations of measurement dynamics facilitate the design of feedback processes. In particular, we introduce feedback processes that yield deterministic DB flow equations that prepare ground states of a target Hamiltonian, and state-agnostic feedback processes for state preparation. We apply the latter for entanglement stabilization of a two-qubit system considering a setup with imperfect measurements and feedback delay. We conclude by re-interpreting feedback processes as gradient flows with tilted fixed points.
tldr: Unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket gradient flows, showing wavefunction collapse as coarse-grained Hamiltonian dynamics or gradient flows.
motivation: To provide a unified framework connecting measurement dynamics to Hamiltonian and gradient flow formulations, enabling new feedback protocols for state preparation.
method: Derives stochastic Hamiltonians that reproduce continuous measurement dynamics, and interprets collapse as double-bracket gradient flows minimizing observable variance.
result: Introduces feedback processes that yield deterministic double-bracket flows for ground state preparation and state-agnostic feedback for entanglement stabilization, demonstrated on a two-qubit system with imperfections.
conclusion: Measurement dynamics can be reinterpreted as Hamiltonian or gradient flows, facilitating design of feedback processes for quantum state preparation and stabilization.

title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: Quantum walks on simplicial complexes are used to encode combinatorial Laplacians and achieve superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis and related problems.
motivation: To explore whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes can provide quantum advantages for topological data analysis and other problems involving higher-order interactions.
method: A novel quantum walk is constructed that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian by operating on a doubled state space of oriented simplices, enabling projection onto harmonic cycles.
result: The construction achieves apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available.
conclusion: Quantum walks on simplicial complexes offer a promising approach for topological data analysis and related problems, with potential applications in computational complexity.

title: Tensor Cross Interpolation Of Purities In Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Dmytro Kolisnyk, Raimel A. Medina, Romain Vasseur, And Maksym Serbyn
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2114 (2026).

A defining feature of quantum many-body systems is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with the number of degrees of freedom. This exponential complexity naïvely renders a complete state characterization, for instance via the complete set of bipartite Renyi entropies for all disjoint regions, a challenging task. Recently, a compact way of storing subregions' purities by encoding them as amplitudes of a fictitious quantum wave function, known as entanglement feature, was proposed. Notably, the entanglement feature can be a simple object even for highly entangled quantum states. However the complexity and practical usage of the entanglement feature for general quantum states has not been explored. In this work, we demonstrate that the entanglement feature can be efficiently learned using only a polynomial amount of samples in the number of degrees of freedom through the so-called tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm, assuming it is expressible as a finite bond dimension MPS. We benchmark this learning process on Haar and random MPS states, confirming analytic expectations. Applying the TCI algorithm to quantum eigenstates of various one dimensional quantum systems, we identify cases where eigenstates have entanglement feature learnable with TCI. We conclude with possible applications of the learned entanglement feature, such as quantifying the distance between different entanglement patterns and finding the optimal one-dimensional ordering of physical indices in a given state, highlighting the potential utility of the proposed purity interpolation method.

.
tldr: This paper uses tensor cross interpolation to efficiently learn the entanglement feature (set of bipartite purities) of quantum many-body states, demonstrating polynomial sample complexity for states with matrix product state structure.
motivation: Characterizing entanglement in many-body systems is exponentially hard; the entanglement feature offers a compact representation, but its practical learning complexity was unknown.
method: The authors apply the tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm to learn the entanglement feature as a matrix product state (MPS) from a polynomial number of samples, benchmarking on Haar random states and random MPS.
result: TCI can efficiently learn the entanglement feature for states that are themselves MPS or have low entanglement feature complexity; they identify eigenstates of 1D systems where this holds.
conclusion: The learned entanglement feature enables quantifying distance between entanglement patterns and finding optimal 1D ordering of indices, suggesting practical utility for entanglement analysis.

title: Operator Delocalization In Disordered Spin Chains Via Exact Mpo Marginals
authors: Jonnathan Pineda-Jiménez, Mario Collura, Gianluca Passarelli, Procolo Lucignano, Davide Rossini And Angelo Russomanno
abstract: We investigate operator delocalization in disordered one-dimensional spin chains by introducing—besides the already known operator mass—a complementary measure of operator complexity: the operator length. Like the operator nonstabilizerness, both these quantities are defined from the expansion of time-evolved operators in the Pauli basis. They characterize, respectively, the number of sites on which an operator acts nontrivially and the spatial extent of its support. We show that both the operator mass and length can be computed efficiently and exactly within a matrix-product-state framework, providing direct access to their full probability distributions, without resorting to stochastic sampling. Applying this approach to the disordered spin-1/2 chain, we find sharply distinct behaviors in non-interacting and interacting regimes. In the Anderson-localized case, operator mass, length, and operator entanglement entropy rapidly saturate, signaling the absence of scrambling. By contrast, in the many-body localized (MBL) regime, for arbitrarily weak interactions, all quantities exhibit a robust logarithmic growth in time, consistent with the known logarithmic light cone of quantum-correlation propagation in MBL. We demonstrate that this behavior is quantitatively captured by an effective -bit model and persists across system sizes accessible via tensor-network simulations.
tldr: This paper studies operator delocalization in disordered spin chains using exact MPO marginals, revealing distinct behaviors in Anderson-localized and many-body localized regimes.
motivation: Understanding operator complexity and scrambling in disordered quantum systems is crucial for characterizing many-body localization and its implications for quantum information processing.
method: The authors introduce operator length as a measure of operator complexity and compute it exactly using matrix-product state (MPS) techniques, avoiding stochastic sampling.
result: In the Anderson-localized phase, operator mass, length, and entanglement entropy saturate rapidly; in the MBL phase, they exhibit robust logarithmic growth, captured by an effective l-bit model.
conclusion: The exact MPO approach provides a powerful tool to study operator delocalization, confirming the logarithmic light cone in MBL and distinguishing it from Anderson localization.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A method for simulating quantum systems with classical stochastic noise using temporal coarse-graining and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with noise that has temporal correlations over many time scales (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging.
method: The noise is expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes; temporal coarse-graining is achieved by conditioning on a coarse realization and analytically averaging over bridge processes.
result: The deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and bridge processes are independent with analytically known correlators, enabling precomputation of noise propagators.
conclusion: The approach provides practical advantages like a simple concatenation rule and is demonstrated with numerical examples.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical circuits that provide necessary conditions for exact and approximate state preparation.
motivation: Understanding the limitations of linear optical state preparation is crucial for generating entangled resources like NOON states without post-selection.
method: Maps the evolution of quantum states under passive linear interferometers onto the Lie algebra of the corresponding Hamiltonians and identifies conserved quantities (e.g., spectrum of the density matrix).
result: Provides invariants that must match for exact state preparation and a lower bound on the distance to a target state based on invariant mismatch.
conclusion: These invariants can be used to rule out impossible linear optical evolutions, guiding future state preparation methods.

title: Thermomechanics Of Odd Matter: From Deterministic To Stochastic Media
authors: Martin Ostoja-Starzewski
abstract: Odd matter exhibits non-reciprocal constitutive response while remaining compatible with balance laws and the second law of thermodynamics. We develop a unified continuum framework based on Edelen’s primitive thermodynamics, which decomposes generalized forces into gradient (hyperdissipative) and orthogonal (powerless) components. We show that this convex decomposition in velocity space admits an elastic analogue: hyperelastic response corresponds to integrable stresses derived from a stored-energy potential, while odd elasticity arises as the non-integrable, yet not derivable from a stored-energy potential branch of admissible response. Within the odd elasticity, we distinguish two cases: an instantaneous power orthogonality (the stronger one) or a configurational orthogonality (the weaker one). Working within the case of configurational orthogonality we construct the (linear) thermo-poromechanical theory, derive a finite strain odd neo-Hookean solid, and establish preservation of coercivity and exponential energy decay in random fluid and solid odd continua. Scale-dependent homogenization preserves coercivity of the even part and orthogonality of the odd part. In driven granular Couette flow, odd stresses modify fluctuation statistics without producing entropy, consistent with the fluctuation theorem. The results provide a systematic thermodynamic foundation for odd matter in deterministic and stochastic settings.
tldr: Develops a thermodynamic framework for odd matter using Edelen's primitive thermodynamics, showing odd elasticity as non-integrable but admissible response.
motivation: Odd matter exhibits non-reciprocal constitutive response, and a unified thermodynamic foundation is needed to reconcile it with balance laws and the second law.
method: Uses convex decomposition of generalized forces into gradient and orthogonal components, and constructs linear thermo-poromechanical theory and finite strain odd neo-Hookean solid.
result: Establishes preservation of coercivity and exponential energy decay in random odd continua; odd stresses in granular Couette flow modify fluctuation statistics without entropy production.
conclusion: Provides a systematic thermodynamic basis for odd matter, linking odd elasticity to non-integrable response while respecting thermodynamics.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: Demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in nanoparticle orientational relaxation and designs protocols to accelerate dynamics by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and overcoming memory effects that limit acceleration of relaxation in stochastic systems with many degrees of freedom.
method: Optical birefringence measurements of field-induced orientation in polydisperse nanoparticle suspensions, analyzed via Smoluchowski equation and multiscale relaxation theory.
result: Kovacs nonmonotonic relaxation observed; memory arises from polydispersity; sequential suppression of slow modes reduces relaxation time significantly.
conclusion: Memory effects in multiscale stochastic dynamics can be mitigated by tailored control protocols, offering a strategy for accelerating relaxation.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proves that wide quantum neural networks with Clifford+Pauli gates cannot achieve quantum advantage by showing their neural tangent kernel can be computed classically.
motivation: To determine whether quantum neural networks can provide a quantum advantage over classical models, specifically by analyzing their training dynamics via the neural tangent kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters in the NTK with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation of the circuit.
result: The NTK of such quantum neural networks can be computed classically in polynomial time, implying that wide networks are equivalent to Gaussian processes and thus classically simulable.
conclusion: Wide quantum neural networks of the considered class cannot achieve quantum advantage, as their expected output can be computed classically.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has an irrational index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that preserve a symmetry, which is a topic in quantum computation theory.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define two topological invariants: an anyon permutation map and a generalized GNVW index, and proves classification up to finite-depth symmetric circuits.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs for finite Abelian group symmetries, and demonstrates that the Kramers-Wannier duality cannot be extended to a full QCA.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous classification of symmetric QCAs, but is primarily a mathematical result in quantum cellular automata theory, not directly aligned with the user's core interests.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement in lossy multi-path atom interferometers using spin-squeezed states, focusing on practical metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin squeezing can improve sensitivity but is degraded by losses and finite temperature.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses from velocity selectivity and scattering, and one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree yields several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite realistic losses.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but finite temperature poses a significant challenge.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) satisfying the Pauli principle and a variable bosonic part.
result: A benchmark lithium wave function with hundreds of basis functions is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five of which are numerically significant.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents an open-source Python library (PyOpticL) for modular optical system design and demonstrates its use for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Conventional optical design is piecewise and not scalable, hindering quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions.
method: Develops PyOpticL, a code-to-CAD tool using beam-path simulation and dynamic routing, and creates modular baseplates for common AMO subsystems.
result: Demonstrates a full laser system for strontium trapped ions achieving over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates.
conclusion: Enables scalable, modular optical systems for quantum computing and other AMO experiments.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies electron trajectories in strong field ionization using squeezed light, focusing on quantum statistics effects on ultrafast dynamics.
motivation: To understand how squeezed light modifies electron dynamics in strong field ionization, potentially offering new control over ultrafast processes.
method: Generalized classical trajectory Monte-Carlo technique to simulate strong field ionization by squeezed states of light.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum; transverse momentum distribution shows varying rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Squeezed light provides additional control over ultrafast electron dynamics, but the atomic potential plays a crucial role.

title: Experimental Exclusion Of A Generalized Károlyházy Gravity-induced Decoherence Model
authors: Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola And Catalina Curceanu
abstract: We report new experimental constraints on the generalized version of the gravity-induced decoherence model originally proposed by Károlyházy. Using data collected by the VIP Collaboration at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory with a high-purity germanium detector, we derive an improved lower bound on the spatial correlation length characterizing metric fluctuations in the model. We obtain a bound m (95% C.L.), which exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the previous experimental limit. When combined with the theoretical upper bound m derived from macroscopic localization requirements, our result excludes the generalized Károlyházy model. The same conclusion applies to an associated non-Markovian formulation of the continuous spontaneous localization model. Our findings significantly tighten experimental constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios and demonstrate the sensitivity of underground low-background experiments to foundational modifications of quantum mechanics.
tldr: Experimental exclusion of a gravity-induced decoherence model using underground detector data.
motivation: To test foundational modifications of quantum mechanics that predict gravity-induced decoherence, which could affect quantum coherence in large systems.
method: Analysis of high-purity germanium detector data from the VIP Collaboration at Gran Sasso, deriving bounds on the spatial correlation length of metric fluctuations.
result: Improved lower bound on the correlation length by over an order of magnitude, excluding the generalized Károlyházy model when combined with theoretical upper bounds.
conclusion: The generalized Károlyházy gravity-induced decoherence model is ruled out, tightening constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios.

title: Random-with-constraints: Constructing Minimal Models For High-dimensional Biology
authors: Ilya Nemenmanpankaj Mehtaahttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Physics, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322bhttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Biology, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322chttps://ror.org/03czfpz43initiative In Theory And Modeling Of Living Systems, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322dhttps://ror.org/05qwgg493department Of Physics, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215ehttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing And Data Science, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
Biologists and physicists have a rich tradition of modeling dynamics of living systems with simple models composed of a few interacting components. Despite the remarkable success of this approach, it remains unclear how to use such finely tuned models to ...
tldr: This paper proposes a method for constructing minimal models of high-dimensional biological systems using random constraints.
motivation: Biologists and physicists often use simple models for complex systems, but it is unclear how to systematically build such models from data.
method: The authors introduce a 'random-with-constraints' framework that generates minimal models by imposing random constraints on model parameters.
result: The approach is demonstrated on biological examples, showing that it can capture essential dynamics while remaining interpretable.
conclusion: The method provides a principled way to construct minimal models for high-dimensional biological systems, bridging data-driven and theory-driven approaches.

title: Estimating The Amount Of Computation Done By A Brain Using Population Neural Activity
authors: Junang Liyuzheng Linanuj Kumar Sharmaandrew M. Leiferdavid H. SignificanceQuantifying the “amount of computation” a dynamic system performs is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to real-world processes like neural activity. We introduce a broadly applicable data-driven framework defining the “amount of ...
tldr: This paper introduces a data-driven framework to estimate the amount of computation performed by a brain based on population neural activity.
motivation: Quantifying computation in dynamic systems like the brain is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to real-world processes.
method: The authors develop a framework that uses population neural activity data to define and estimate the 'amount of computation'.
result: The framework provides a way to measure computation in neural systems, with potential applications in neuroscience and complex systems.
conclusion: The work offers a novel approach to bridging computation theory and neural dynamics, but is not directly aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Direct Derivation Of The Modified Langevin Noise Formalism From The Canonical Quantization Of Macroscopic Electromagnetism
authors: A Ciattoni
abstract: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models the interaction of the quantized electromagnetic field with an arbitrary lossy magneto-dielectric object placed in vacuum using three types of non-interacting bosonic polaritons: scattering, electric, and magnetic. These respectively represent free-space photons scattered by the object, and photons radiated by quantized electric and magnetic dipolar sources embedded within its volume. Recently (Ciattoni 2024 Phys. Rev. A110 013707), this formalism was justified from the canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) (Philbin 2010 New J. Phys.12 123008) in the Heisenberg picture. This was achieved by identifying the polariton operators within the formal solution of the macroscopic Maxwell equations, assuming they obey bosonic commutation relations to retrieve the canonical ones, and showing they diagonalize the CQME Hamiltonian. However, the explicit functional dependence of these polaritons on the underlying canonical field operators remained undetermined. In this paper, we derive the exact analytical expressions for the polariton operators in terms of the canonical CQME field operators. Using these mappings, we provide a direct and rigorous derivation of the MLNF from the canonical theory in the Schrödinger picture. Our derivation is structured in three foundational steps: 1) adopting the derived analytical expressions as the constitutive definitions of the polariton operators; 2) mathematically proving that these operators are strictly bosonic as a direct consequence of the canonical commutation relations; and 3) demonstrating that they exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian.
tldr: This paper derives explicit analytical expressions for polariton operators in the modified Langevin noise formalism from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism.
motivation: To provide a rigorous derivation of the modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) by finding the explicit mapping between polariton operators and canonical field operators.
method: The authors derive exact analytical expressions for scattering, electric, and magnetic polariton operators in terms of the canonical CQME field operators, then prove they satisfy bosonic commutation relations and diagonalize the Hamiltonian.
result: The polariton operators are shown to be strictly bosonic and to exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian, providing a direct derivation of MLNF from CQME in the Schrödinger picture.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous foundation for the modified Langevin noise formalism, confirming its consistency with canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism.

title: A Frequency-domain Identifiability Law For Deterministic Reconstruction Of Complex Networks Under Partial Observability
authors: Tianlong Fan And Linyuan Lü Xiaoxiao Liang
abstract: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is central to computational studies of complex systems, with implications for detecting covert actors in terrorist networks, localizing unobserved brain regions, and revealing latent molecular regulators. Focusing on evolutionary game dynamics, we uncover an empirically consistent frequency-domain regularity: the aggregated magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a node’s payoff time series scales linearly with its structural degree, , across tested topologies and parameter regimes. Leveraging this structure–behavior scaling, we develop a deterministic inference framework that (i) estimates degrees directly from DFT spectra via a single global-slope fit, and (ii) uses brief, identifiability-oriented local interventions (‘suppress-and-measure’) to reveal adjacencies through intervention-induced spectral drops. Discrepancies between estimated degree and revealed neighbors deterministically enumerate external edges to hidden components and yield tight lower/upper bounds on the number of unobserved nodes. We analyze the conditions under which the scaling holds, quantify deviations under structural heterogeneity, and characterize sample-length dependence. Experiments on synthetic and empirical networks demonstrate accurate topology recovery, robustness to stochasticity, and scalability to thousand-node graphs, with consistent gains over causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines. These results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into actionable structural information.
tldr: This paper uses DFT of payoff time series to infer network structure from partial observations in evolutionary game dynamics.
motivation: Inferring hidden network architecture from limited behavioral data is important for detecting covert actors, unobserved brain regions, or latent molecular regulators.
method: The authors discover a linear scaling between the aggregated DFT magnitude of a node's payoff time series and its degree, then use a global-slope fit to estimate degrees and a 'suppress-and-measure' intervention to reveal adjacencies.
result: The method accurately recovers topology in synthetic and empirical networks, outperforms baselines, and provides bounds on the number of unobserved nodes.
conclusion: The DFT-based approach offers a deterministic, scalable route to structure discovery under partial observability.

title: Photon Accelerator In Magnetized Electron–ion Plasma
authors: S V Bulanov, S S Bulanov, T Z Esirkepov, G Gregori, G M Grittani, M Lamač, B K Russell, A G R Thomas And P Valenta
abstract: Strong magnetic fields and plasmas are intrinsically linked in both terrestrial laboratory experiments and in space phenomena. One of the most profound consequences of that is the change in relationship between the frequency and the wave number of electromagnetic waves propagating in plasma in the presence of such magnetic fields when compared to the case without these fields. Furthermore, magnetic fields alter electromagnetic wave interaction with relativistic plasma waves, resulting in different outcomes for particle and radiation generation. For a relativistic plasma wave-based photon acceleration this leads to an increased frequency gain and, thus, potentially to higher efficiency. The influence of a magnetic field leads to quantitative and qualitative change in the properties of photon acceleration, amplifying the increase in the electromagnetic wave frequency.
tldr: This paper studies photon acceleration in magnetized electron-ion plasma, focusing on frequency upshifts due to relativistic plasma waves and magnetic fields.
motivation: To understand how strong magnetic fields affect photon acceleration in plasma, which is relevant to laboratory and astrophysical plasmas.
method: Theoretical analysis using plasma physics and wave equations to model photon acceleration in the presence of a magnetic field.
result: Magnetic fields enhance the frequency gain of photons interacting with relativistic plasma waves, leading to higher efficiency.
conclusion: The presence of magnetic fields qualitatively and quantitatively changes photon acceleration, potentially enabling more efficient frequency upshifts.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and symmetry properties.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the propagation and stability of vortex light states.
method: The authors introduce disclinations into Penrose-tiling quasicrystals to create structures with arbitrary discrete rotational symmetry, then numerically solve the nonlinear Schrödinger equation to find linear eigenmodes and soliton families.
result: They discover two classes of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with in-phase or out-of-phase bright spot pairs, and find that low-charge vortices can be stable, with stability intervals widening as rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: Disclination quasicrystals enrich the linear spectrum and support novel stable vortex solitons, extending localization theory to topologically deformed quasicrystals.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on magnetoelastic coupling and lattice stiffening.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic orders in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice contraction and dramatic stiffening of the lattice (Young's modulus increase by ~10 GPa).
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, possibly due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. title: Nucleation Of Adamantane Clusters In Weakly Ionised Plasmas: Dispersion Cohesion, Surface Energy, And Charging
authors: Johannes Fiedler And Justas Zalieckas
abstract: The formation of molecular clusters in low-temperature plasmas is governed by an intricate interplay of dispersion interactions, electrostatic charging, and surface energetics. While chemical growth pathways have been extensively studied, the role of non-chemical interactions in determining characteristic cluster sizes remains poorly understood. In this work, we develop a unified free-energy framework for molecular clusters embedded in weakly ionised Ar/H plasmas. The approach combines first-principles calculations of the molecular polarisability of adamantane with a dielectric description of the plasma response, including collisional damping and plasma screening. Dispersion interactions are treated as a bulk-like cohesive contribution with a physically motivated microscopic cutoff, while electrostatic charging is described within floating-potential theory. We show that, for realistic discharge parameters, the total free energy does not generally exhibit an effective equilibrium radius. Instead, the free-energy landscape is characterised by a nucleation barrier with an effective critical radius separating subcritical clusters from downhill growth. By mapping this nucleation threshold scale as a function of pressure, electron temperature, and gas composition, we demonstrate that plasma conditions provide a systematic control over the nucleation scale. Our results suggest that experimentally observed steady cluster sizes in weakly ionised plasmas are governed by kinetic balance rather than free-energy minimisation, and that gas composition and plasma parameters can be used as effective control knobs for early-stage cluster formation.
tldr: This paper studies the nucleation of adamantane clusters in weakly ionized plasmas using a free-energy framework, focusing on dispersion interactions and charging effects.
motivation: To understand the role of non-chemical interactions in determining cluster sizes in low-temperature plasmas, which is poorly understood.
method: Develops a unified free-energy model combining first-principles polarisability calculations with a dielectric plasma description, including collisional damping and screening.
result: The free-energy landscape shows a nucleation barrier with a critical radius; no equilibrium radius exists; cluster sizes are governed by kinetic balance.
conclusion: Plasma conditions (pressure, electron temperature, gas composition) can control nucleation scale, but steady cluster sizes arise from kinetics, not free-energy minimization.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics

abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for analyzing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand nontrivial physics beyond planarity in gauge/gravity duality by studying correlators involving giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden defect extension of 10d conformal symmetry and extracts the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel double-particle operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

title: Orthogonal Phase Modulation And Lissajous Mode Decoupling In Light-induced Thermoelastic Spectroscopy For Real-time Multi-component Gas Sensing
authors: Hanxu Ma, Shunda Qiao, Ying He, Haiyue Sun And Yufei Ma
abstract: This paper proposed an optical detection mechanism that utilized orthogonal phase modulation (OPM) and Lissajous mode decoupling within a light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES) sensor for the first time, enabling real-time multi-component gas sensing. By establishing a two-dimensional forced vibration model of a quartz tuning fork (QTF) under dual-path OPM, it revealed the vibration mode coupling mechanism induced by non-ideal phase and amplitude conditions, thereby providing a theoretical basis and optimization pathway for suppressing channel crosstalk. In the OPM-LITES sensor, two continuous-wave distributed feedback lasers were modulated by sinusoidal waves with the same frequency (f0/2, where f0 is the resonant frequency of the QTF) but a phase difference of 45°. The combined beam, after wavelength division multiplexing, co-excited the self-designed low-frequency QTF. The piezoelectric signal generated by the QTF underwent orthogonal demodulation via a lock-in amplifier (LIA). The concentration information for the two gases was independently retrieved from the decoupled X-component and Y-component of the LIA. Experimental results demonstrated that the OPM-LITES sensor exhibited excellent linear responses to both methane (CH4) and acetylene (C2H2), with average relative systematic errors of 0.54% and 0.79%, and maximum relative errors of 1.72% and 1.38%, respectively. Allan deviation analysis indicated that the minimum detection limits (MDLs) for CH4 and C2H2 reached 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, with normalized noise-equivalent absorption coefficients of 5.09 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2 and 6.18 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2, respectively. This study not only provided a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection but also established a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling and signal processing in spectroscopic sensing.

method: Two lasers are modulated with same frequency but 45° phase difference, co-excite a quartz tuning fork, and the piezoelectric signal is orthogonally demodulated via lock-in amplifier to decouple gas concentration information.
result: The sensor achieves linear responses for CH4 and C2H2 with low systematic errors (0.54% and 0.79%) and detection limits of 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm respectively.
conclusion: The proposed OPM-LITES sensor provides a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection with a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling.
